summary:
Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla has no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity statute. An index of Spain's regional LGTBI legislation states expressly that Melilla and Ceuta have no laws of this kind and rely instead on the national framework and on central-government equality policies. The city therefore stands entirely under Spanish national law for legal gender recognition, anti-discrimination protection, criminal aggravating circumstances and access to facilities, and no city-level rule either adds to or subtracts from those guarantees.

The only city-level instrument touching partnership recognition is a registry for unmarried couples, created in Melilla in 2008. Comparable registries exist in Ceuta and across the mainland communities, and the benefits they confer on unmarried couples are regarded as mainly symbolic. The Melilla registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity statute and does not modify the national rules on marriage or adoption, so a trans visitor's recognition as a partner or spouse rests on the national framework rather than on anything the city has enacted.
tangentialFactors:
Melilla's position is shared with Ceuta, the other autonomous city: neither has produced an autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity law, and both depend on the national framework and central-government equality policies. Within the two autonomous cities there is no regional comparator offering a stronger or weaker statutory standard.

Because no autonomous statute exists, the level of protection available in Melilla moves with national legislation rather than with any city-level legislative programme; the index of regional LGTBI laws records no Melilla enactment to track.

The 2008 unmarried-couples registry places Melilla within a wider pattern of similar registers adopted by Ceuta and the mainland communities, in which the practical value to couples is limited and symbolic rather than a source of substantive rights.
localsOnly:
Residents of Melilla have no autonomous LGTBI or gender-identity legislation to invoke before city authorities, and no city-level statute to amend; they rely on the national framework and on central-government equality policies for protection in healthcare, employment, housing and criminal proceedings.

Unmarried couples resident in the city may register under the 2008 municipal registry for unmarried couples. The benefits attached to that registration are regarded as mainly symbolic, and the registry is not an LGTBI or gender-identity instrument.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory contains no Melilla-specific enforcement data, prosecutions, incident reports or trans-specific violence figures. Whether the national aggravating circumstances for gender-identity motives are applied in Melilla courts, and at what rate, is not sourced.

The practical operation of the 2008 unmarried-couples registry is not detailed in the sources: eligibility conditions, the specific benefits conferred and how a relationship locally classified as same-sex is handled at registration are unresolved.

How central-government equality policies are delivered at the local level in Melilla, and through which city or state bodies, is not described in the available material.
